conflict_topics: who is responsible for ventilating when cooking (normative rule)
moving personal drying rack without prior consent
access to the single stove (timing of handover)
extractor fan noise interfering with Agent C's upcoming tutoring
dialogue_quality_notes: Agents give concrete reasons (rain on laundry, tutoring noise, risk of ruining food) which guide pragmatic compromises.
One agent moved another's drying rack without prior consent, prompting an explicit request to check in future — shows partial role confusion around shared vs personal space.
Participants coordinate on timing (explicit minute counts) which helps manage the shared stove despite unresolved policy.
evaluation.final_reason: Immediate practical frictions were addressed (extractor turned on, drying rack moved, stove freed), and participants made commitments (D to lower extractor, B to open window). However the normative dispute over a standing rule assigning ventilation responsibility was never settled, and some promised actions (window opening, lowering extractor) were not all confirmed before the transcript ended.
position_change_notes: Agent A: retained opposition to an on-the-spot standing rule but conceded practically by agreeing to free the stove after the cooking completes.
Agent B: initially insisted on immediate ventilation responsibility but pragmatically moved the rack and offered to open the window; however, B did so without prior consent from C (later addressed).
Agent C: did not block the rack move but asserted a preference for future notice and requested extractor adjustment for an upcoming tutoring session.
Agent D: consistently cooperative — turned on extractor early and agreed to lower/turn it off once the stove is freed.

round_scores.evidence: Existing disagreement about who must ventilate and a proposed standing rule (B vs A) is active. Agent A refuses the imposed rule; Agent D turns on the extractor fan as a mitigating action.

Agent B moves Agent C's drying rack (action taken without C's prior consent) to enable opening the window; Agent A agrees to free the stove in ~8 minutes. Immediate practical barrier to ventilation is removed, but consent/ownership and the standing-rule dispute remain unresolved.

Agent C raises the noise concern (extractor hum) and requests future notice before moving the rack; Agent D agrees to check with C and to turn off/lower the extractor after A frees the stove. Tensions reduce via commitments, but the underlying rule dispute about who must ventilate remains.

No new statements or actions. Cooking continues; extractor is on and laundry is protected. The practical situation is stable, but the normative question of a standing ventilation rule is still unsettled.

Agent D waits and promises to lower the extractor when A frees the stove; Agent A promises to step away in ~2 minutes. Cooperative coordination reduces immediate friction; outstanding policy disagreement persists but is currently minor.

Agent A releases the stove and asks Agent B to open the window; A physically frees the stove. Window opening and extractor lowering are requested/promised but not confirmed, and the broader standing-rule dispute remains unsettled.

substantive_insights: Practical, time-limited accommodations (turning on extractor, moving rack temporarily) can de-escalate an acute shared-resource conflict even when the underlying normative rule is unsettled.

Consent around personal property (drying rack) is a distinct tension from the ventilation-responsibility dispute; resolving the immediate hazard (rain) does not settle consent norms for future actions.

Noise trade-offs (extractor hum vs odour) create competing priorities—mitigation for one party (turning on extractor) can impose costs on another (interfering with C's tutoring), requiring layered accommodations.
